---
title: "Sparse PK Sampling"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(PKNCA)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
conflicted::conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter, dplyr::select, .quiet = TRUE)
```

## What is sparse PK?

In **dense PK**, each subject contributes a full concentration-time profile. In **sparse PK**, each subject (usually an animal) contributes only one or a few samples, so there is no individual profile to analyze. Instead, the samples of all animals in a group are pooled into one profile, and the parameters describe that group.

Holder et al. (1999) describe three sampling designs:

- **Serial sacrifice** (destructive sampling): each animal is sampled once, typically at necropsy, with a few animals at each timepoint. This is the usual toxicokinetic design in rodents.
- **Batch**: animals are divided into batches, and each animal in a batch is sampled at the same subset of the timepoints, so each animal gives two or three samples but no animal gives the whole profile.
- **Complete**: every animal is sampled at every timepoint. Such data can be analyzed as dense data, one animal at a time, or pooled as sparse data.

PKNCA handles all three with the same code: give `sparse = TRUE` to `PKNCAconc()` and request the parameters by their usual names. Two things happen behind that flag:

1. The AUC and AUMC parameters that have a sparse estimator (`auclast`, `aucall`, `aucinf.obs`, `aumclast`, `aumcall`, `aumcinf.obs`, and after an IV bolus the `auciv*` and `aumciv*` equivalents) are calculated from the pooled samples with the Bailer (1988) point estimate and the Nedelman–Jia/Holder standard error. Each reports a standard error and degrees of freedom alongside it, with the suffixes `_se` and `_df` (for example, `auclast_se` and `auclast_df`) (≥ 0.13.0).
2. Every other parameter (Cmax, Tmax, half-life, and so on) is calculated from the **arithmetic-mean profile** of the animals in the group.

See also the package vignette [Sparse NCA Calculations](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v04-sparse.html). The AUC to infinity, its standard error with the uncertainty of λz, and IV bolus dosing are covered in the next chapter, [Sparse AUC to Infinity and Its Uncertainty](sparse-uncertainty.qmd).

---

## Dataset: serial sacrifice design

The example is a simulated oral study: 7 timepoints with 4 animals sacrificed at each (28 animals, one sample each). As is usual for sacrificial designs, no animal is sampled at the time of the dose.

```{r}
set.seed(42)

# One-compartment oral model (ka and kel in 1/h, dose in mg, v in L)
pk_conc <- function(t, ka = 1.5, kel = 0.15, dose = 100, v = 50) {
  (dose / v) * (ka / (ka - kel)) * (exp(-kel * t) - exp(-ka * t))
}

d_serial <- data.frame(time = rep(c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24), each = 4))
# Every animal needs its own identifier, even with one sample per animal
d_serial$animal <- seq_len(nrow(d_serial))
d_serial$conc <- signif(pk_conc(d_serial$time) * exp(rnorm(nrow(d_serial), sd = 0.25)), 3)

head(d_serial, 8)
```

```{r}
ggplot(d_serial, aes(x = time, y = conc)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "black") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "black", shape = 18) +
  labs(
    title = "Serial sacrifice: individual samples (grey) and mean profile (black)",
    x = "Time (h)", y = "Concentration (mg/L)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Subject (animal) identifiers are required even when every animal gives one sample, because which animal contributed which samples changes the standard error. With one sample per animal, a sequential number is enough, as above.

---

## The sparse workflow

```{r}
# Concentration object: flag the data as sparse
o_conc <- PKNCAconc(d_serial, conc ~ time | animal, sparse = TRUE)

# Dose object: one row with no groups applies to every animal
d_dose <- data.frame(dose = 100, time = 0)
o_dose <- PKNCAdose(d_dose, dose ~ time)

# Data object: the usual parameter names, and a zero imputed at time 0
o_data <- PKNCAdata(
  o_conc, o_dose,
  intervals = data.frame(
    start = 0, end = 24,
    auclast = TRUE, aumclast = TRUE, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, half.life = TRUE
  ),
  impute = "start_conc0"
)

o_nca <- pk.nca(o_data)
as.data.frame(o_nca) |>
  select(PPTESTCD, PPORRES)
```

There is one row per parameter for the group, not one per animal. `auclast_se`, `auclast_df`, `aumclast_se`, and `aumclast_df` are reported although they were not requested, because the sparse estimator returns all three together. They can also be requested on their own; requesting them for dense data is an error ("This parameter is only calculated for sparse PK").

`pk.nca()` prints a message that the `auc.method` option does not apply to the sparse estimators. The sparse variance is derived for a fixed-weight linear combination of the means, so the sparse estimators always use the linear trapezoidal rule, whatever `auc.method` says (its default is `"lin up/log down"`). Parameters calculated from the mean profile do follow `auc.method`.

### A concentration at time 0

As for any AUC in PKNCA, the sparse AUC needs a concentration at the start of the interval, measured or imputed. Without one, the AUC and its standard error and degrees of freedom are `NA`:

```{r}
o_nca_no_c0 <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(
  o_conc, o_dose,
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 24, auclast = TRUE)
))
as.data.frame(o_nca_no_c0) |>
  select(PPTESTCD, PPORRES)
```

The warning ("Requesting an AUC range starting (0) before the first measurement (0.5) is not allowed") explains the `NA`. After an extravascular dose, impute a zero with `impute = "start_conc0"`, as in the first example (≥ 0.13.0; see [Concentration Imputation](imputation.qmd)). The imputed zero is known rather than measured, so it has weight in the estimate but adds nothing to the variance or the degrees of freedom. A pre-dose sample measured as zero works the same way. Other imputations (such as `start_predose`) give estimates whose uncertainty the sparse estimators cannot include, so when they would add a concentration to the pooled samples, `pk.nca()` stops with the `pknca_error_sparse_impute` error. After an IV bolus, request the IV parameters instead; they back-extrapolate C0 from the mean profile (see [Sparse AUC to Infinity and Its Uncertainty](sparse-uncertainty.qmd#iv-bolus-c0)).

`pknca_interval_table()` (≥ 0.13.0) has a `sparse_single_dose` preset that requests a single-dose parameter set with the `start_conc0` imputation:

```{r}
d_preset <- pknca_interval_table(0, Inf, preset = "sparse_single_dose")
names(d_preset)[vapply(d_preset, isTRUE, logical(1))]
d_preset$impute
```

See [Interval Selection and Parameter Catalog](intervals.qmd) for interval specifications in general.

---

## The mean profile and BLQ samples

The mean profile is the arithmetic mean of the samples at each timepoint, with one rule for samples below the limit of quantification (BLQ, coded as 0): if **strictly more than 50%** of the samples at a timepoint are BLQ, the mean at that timepoint is set to 0. At exactly 50% BLQ, the mean is calculated normally, with the BLQ values as 0. This method (`"arithmetic mean, <=50% BLQ"`) is not a user-facing option.

To see the rule, censor the serial data at an LLOQ of 0.06 mg/L, which makes 3 of the 4 samples at 24 h BLQ. `sparse_mean()` calculates the mean profile from an `as_sparse_pk()` object:

```{r}
d_blq <- d_serial |>
  mutate(lloq = 0.06, conc = ifelse(conc < lloq, 0, conc))

sp <- sparse_mean(as_sparse_pk(conc = d_blq$conc, time = d_blq$time, subject = d_blq$animal))
data.frame(
  time = vapply(sp, `[[`, numeric(1), "time"),
  n_blq = vapply(sp, function(x) sum(x$conc == 0), numeric(1)),
  mean = vapply(sp, `[[`, numeric(1), "mean")
)
```

The 24 h mean is zero although one animal had a measurable concentration, so tlast becomes 12 h. The sparse AUClast stops at tlast, and the times after tlast do not contribute to its standard error or degrees of freedom either (≥ 0.13.0). The `conc.blq` option applies as for dense data (see [Utility Functions](utilities.qmd)), and per-run `options` in `PKNCAdata()` reach the sparse estimators the same way as global `PKNCA.options()` settings. Missing (`NA`) concentrations are dropped.

---

## Confidence intervals

The standard error and degrees of freedom give a *t*-based confidence interval:

```{r}
d_res <- as.data.frame(o_nca)
auc <- d_res$PPORRES[d_res$PPTESTCD == "auclast"]
se  <- d_res$PPORRES[d_res$PPTESTCD == "auclast_se"]
df  <- d_res$PPORRES[d_res$PPTESTCD == "auclast_df"]

ci <- auc + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df) * se
sprintf("AUClast = %.2f, 95%% CI: %.2f to %.2f (df = %.1f)", auc, ci[1], ci[2], df)
```

With serial sacrifice, the degrees of freedom are the Satterthwaite approximation of Nedelman, Gibiansky, and Lau (1995). They are not the number of animals minus one: here, with `r nrow(d_serial)` animals, `auclast_df` is `r round(df, 1)`. They are `NA` when a timepoint has a single animal, because its variance cannot be estimated.

---

## The summary shows the estimate and its standard error

```{r}
summary(o_nca)
```

In `summary()`, a sparse AUC or AUMC is shown as the estimate with its standard error in brackets (≥ 0.13.0); the caption says "estimate and standard error", and `auclast_se` gets no column of its own. (In PKNCA 0.12.1, the single sparse estimate was described as a geometric mean with a geometric coefficient of variation.) Each standard error describes one estimate, so a summary row that would combine more than one sparse estimate (for example, after `drop_group` removes the group that separates them) is the `pknca_error_summary_multiple_spread` error.

This pairing is set with the `spread_for` argument of `PKNCA.set.summary()` (≥ 0.13.0): the summary instructions registered for `auclast_se` have `spread_for = "auclast"`, so `auclast` is summarized with the `point` function applied to its values and the `spread` function applied to the `auclast_se` values. The same argument lets a custom parameter be summarized with the spread from another parameter. See [Post-Processing Results](postprocessing.qmd) for summary settings in general.

---

## Derived parameters

Because the sparse estimate is stored under the standard parameter name, every parameter derived from an AUC picks it up by name (≥ 0.13.0): `cl.last` divides the dose by the sparse `auclast`, `mrt.last` divides `aumclast` by `auclast`, `cl.obs` divides the dose by the sparse `aucinf.obs`, and so on down the usual derived graph.

```{r}
o_nca_derived <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(
  o_conc, o_dose,
  intervals = data.frame(
    start = 0, end = Inf,
    aumclast = TRUE, cl.last = TRUE, mrt.last = TRUE, kel.last = TRUE,
    vss.last = TRUE, vz.last = TRUE, lambda.z = TRUE,
    cl.obs = TRUE, mrt.obs = TRUE, vz.obs = TRUE
  ),
  impute = "start_conc0"
))

as.data.frame(o_nca_derived) |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("auclast", "aumclast", "aucinf.obs", "aumcinf.obs", "lambda.z",
                         "cl.last", "mrt.last", "kel.last", "vss.last", "vz.last",
                         "cl.obs", "mrt.obs", "vz.obs")) |>
  select(PPTESTCD, PPORRES)
```

Points to note:

- `kel.last`, like the rest of PKNCA's `kel` family, is `1/MRT`, not the terminal rate constant. Request `lambda.z` for that.
- `vz.last` is the clearance divided by `lambda.z` fitted to the mean profile, the standard toxicokinetic approach. It is `NA` when the mean profile has too few points after its peak to fit λz.
- The derived parameters have no `_se` or `_df` companions. For their uncertainty, use the [bootstrap](#bootstrap-for-any-parameter).
- With extravascular data such as these, the clearance and volume values are apparent (CL/F, V/F).

---

## Half-life of the mean profile

The half-life is fitted to the mean profile, with the same automatic point selection as for dense data (see [Half-Life and Terminal Phase](halflife.qmd)). It describes the population mean curve, which is not the half-life of a typical animal: the late means are dominated by the animals that eliminate slowly, and BLQ samples counted as zero pull the late means down (see the [recommendations](sparse-uncertainty.qmd#practical-recommendations)).

The Tobit half-life (`hl_method = "tobit"`) works for sparse data (≥ 0.13.0). Give the LLOQ with the `lloq` argument of `PKNCAconc()`; the mean profile carries the median LLOQ of the samples at each timepoint, so a timepoint whose mean is set to zero is treated as censored at the LLOQ rather than dropped:

```{r}
o_conc_blq <- PKNCAconc(d_blq, conc ~ time | animal, sparse = TRUE, lloq = "lloq")
d_hl_interval <- data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, half.life = TRUE)

d_hl <- bind_rows(
  `log-linear` = as.data.frame(pk.nca(PKNCAdata(o_conc_blq, o_dose, intervals = d_hl_interval))),
  tobit = as.data.frame(pk.nca(PKNCAdata(
    o_conc_blq, o_dose, intervals = d_hl_interval,
    options = list(hl_method = "tobit")
  ))),
  .id = "hl_method"
)
d_hl |>
  filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("half.life", "lambda.z.time.last", "lambda.z.n.points", "lambda.z.n.points_blq")) |>
  select(hl_method, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = hl_method, values_from = PPORRES)
```

The log-linear fit stops at the 12 h tlast; the Tobit fit also uses the censored 24 h mean. The delta-method standard error of the AUC to infinity needs the log-linear half-life: with `hl_method = "tobit"`, `aucinf.obs_se` and `aucinf.obs_df` are `NA` with the `pknca_warning_sparse_lambda_z_se_hl_method` warning, unless `sparse_lambda_z_se = "none"` (see the [next chapter](sparse-uncertainty.qmd)).

---

## Batch designs

In a batch design, each animal gives several samples. The example has three batches of 4 animals, each batch sampled at two or three of the timepoints:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
d_batch_times <- data.frame(batch = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3), time = c(0.5, 4, 24, 1, 8, 2, 12))
d_batch <- merge(data.frame(batch = rep(1:3, each = 4), animal = 1:12), d_batch_times)
d_batch$conc <- signif(pk_conc(d_batch$time) * exp(rnorm(nrow(d_batch), sd = 0.25)), 3)

# Number of animals sampled at each time, by batch
table(d_batch$batch, d_batch$time)
```

The code is the same as for serial sacrifice:

```{r}
o_conc_batch <- PKNCAconc(d_batch, conc ~ time | animal, sparse = TRUE)
o_nca_batch <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(
  o_conc_batch, o_dose,
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 24, auclast = TRUE, aumclast = TRUE),
  impute = "start_conc0"
))
as.data.frame(o_nca_batch) |>
  select(PPTESTCD, PPORRES)
```

Samples from the same animal are correlated. The standard error includes their covariance with the unbiased estimator of Holder (2001), and the degrees of freedom are the Satterthwaite approximation of Nedelman and Jia (1998, equation 6). Before PKNCA 0.13.0, the degrees of freedom were `NA` with a warning whenever an animal gave more than one sample; they are now calculated, and they match the PK package for batch designs and the published example of Nedelman and Jia (1998).

---

## How animals are grouped

Sparse parameters are calculated from the pooled samples of every animal in the same group. The groups are the grouping variables on the right of `|` in the `PKNCAconc()` formula **with the subject removed**. With `conc ~ time | animal`, removing `animal` leaves no grouping variables, so all of the data form one group. With `conc ~ time | study + treatment + animal`, the animals are pooled within each combination of `study` and `treatment`. The subject does not have to be in the formula: `PKNCAconc(d, conc ~ time | treatment, subject = "animal", sparse = TRUE)` pools by `treatment`. (Before PKNCA 0.13.0, such data were rejected as duplicates when different animals shared a sampling time.)

All animals in a group must share the same dosing; if they do not, PKNCA stops with an error naming the group. See [How Subjects Are Grouped for Sparse Calculations](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v04-sparse.html#how-subjects-are-grouped-for-sparse-calculations) in the vignette.

---

## Bootstrap for any parameter

The standard errors above exist only for the AUC and AUMC families. `sparse_bootstrap()` (≥ 0.13.0) gives uncertainty for every parameter, including Cmax, the half-life, the derived parameters, and ratios between groups. It implements the stratified nonparametric bootstrap of Shen and Machado (2017): animals are resampled with replacement within each set of sampling times (each timepoint with serial sacrifice, each batch in a batch design), keeping each animal's samples together, and every replicate is calculated exactly as the original data are. It returns a sparse `PKNCAconc` object with the original data and the replicates as a new group column (`bootstrap` by default, with the values `"original"` and `"bootstrap1"`, `"bootstrap2"`, ...), and it stores the random seed so that the replicates can be reproduced.

The default is `n_boot = 200` replicates, enough for the mean and standard deviation (Takemoto et al. 2006); percentile intervals need more to be stable. To render quickly, this example uses 50:

```{r}
o_conc_boot <- sparse_bootstrap(o_conc, n_boot = 50, seed = 20261010)
o_data_boot <- PKNCAdata(
  o_conc_boot, o_dose,
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 24, auclast = TRUE, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, half.life = TRUE),
  impute = "start_conc0",
  # Many replicate groups would otherwise show a progress bar
  options = list(progress = FALSE)
)
o_nca_boot <- pk.nca(o_data_boot)
summary(o_nca_boot)
```

`pk.nca()` returns a `PKNCAresults_sparse_bootstrap` object. Its `summary()` treats the replicates the way the summary of dense data treats subjects, with each parameter's usual summary statistics (here, for example, the geometric mean and geometric CV of the replicates' AUClast). `N` is the number of animals in the study, and the caption gives the number of replicates and the seed. `as.data.frame()` has every replicate, including the `"original"` one with the estimates, so the bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of the replicates:

```{r}
d_boot <- as.data.frame(o_nca_boot)
d_boot_original <- d_boot |>
  filter(bootstrap == "original") |>
  select(PPTESTCD, original = PPORRES)
d_boot |>
  filter(bootstrap != "original", PPTESTCD %in% c("auclast", "cmax", "half.life")) |>
  group_by(PPTESTCD) |>
  summarise(
    bootstrap_se = sd(PPORRES),
    lower_95 = quantile(PPORRES, 0.025),
    upper_95 = quantile(PPORRES, 0.975)
  ) |>
  left_join(d_boot_original, by = "PPTESTCD")
```

The bootstrap standard error of `auclast` (`r signif(sd(d_boot$PPORRES[d_boot$bootstrap != "original" & d_boot$PPTESTCD == "auclast"]), 3)`) is smaller than the analytical `auclast_se` (`r signif(d_res$PPORRES[d_res$PPTESTCD == "auclast_se"], 3)`). Resampling *n* animals understates the variance of their mean by the factor (*n* − 1)/*n* (3/4 with 4 animals per timepoint), so with few animals per timepoint the bootstrap intervals are too narrow. Prefer the analytical standard errors for the AUCs, and use the bootstrap for parameters and comparisons that have none; see the [recommendations](sparse-uncertainty.qmd#practical-recommendations).

### Comparing groups with `be_assess()`

`be_assess()` accepts bootstrap results. The ratio of the test and reference estimates (from the `"original"` replicate) is the point estimate, and its confidence interval is the percentile interval of the replicate ratios (90% by default), judged against the acceptance limits; only the `"ABE"` and `"descriptive"` frameworks apply, because a sparse bootstrap has no within-subject variability. In this parallel design, the animals of each formulation are resampled independently:

```{r}
set.seed(5)
d_two <- bind_rows(
  mutate(d_serial, formulation = "reference"),
  mutate(d_serial, formulation = "test", animal = animal + 100,
         conc = signif(conc * exp(rnorm(n(), mean = log(0.9), sd = 0.1)), 3))
)
o_conc_two <- PKNCAconc(d_two, conc ~ time | formulation + animal, sparse = TRUE,
                        concu = "mg/L", timeu = "h")
o_dose_two <- PKNCAdose(data.frame(formulation = c("reference", "test"), dose = 100, time = 0),
                        dose ~ time | formulation, doseu = "mg")
o_nca_two <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(
  sparse_bootstrap(o_conc_two, n_boot = 50, seed = 20261011), o_dose_two,
  intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = 24, auclast = TRUE, cmax = TRUE),
  impute = "start_conc0", options = list(progress = FALSE)
))
o_be <- be_assess(o_nca_two, reference_col = "formulation", reference_value = "reference",
                  endpoints = c("auclast", "cmax"))
o_be
```

The test/reference ratio of AUClast is `r sprintf("%.1f", o_be$gmr_percent[o_be$endpoint == "auclast"])`% with a 90% interval of `r sprintf("%.1f", o_be$ci_lower[o_be$endpoint == "auclast"])`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", o_be$ci_upper[o_be$endpoint == "auclast"])`%, within the 80% to 125% limits; the Cmax interval (`r sprintf("%.1f", o_be$ci_lower[o_be$endpoint == "cmax"])`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", o_be$ci_upper[o_be$endpoint == "cmax"])`%) is not. `n` counts the animals of both formulations.

For a crossover, where each animal receives every treatment, give the treatment column as `paired` to `sparse_bootstrap()` (for example, `paired = "treatment"`), so that each replicate draws the same animals for every treatment. Analytes (the groups after `/` in the formula) are always resampled together. See the [sparse sampling section](bioequivalence.qmd#be-from-sparse-sampling-the-bootstrap-route) of the [Bioequivalence](bioequivalence.qmd) chapter for a paired example and the regulatory context, and the [Bootstrap](https://humanpred.github.io/pknca/articles/v04-sparse.html#bootstrap) section of the vignette.

---

## Sparse parameters

The parameters with a sparse estimator (registered with `FUN_sparse` in `add.interval.col()`), and the sparse-only parameters (which need `sparse = TRUE`), are listed by the parameter registry. The deprecated names (below) are left out:

```{r}
cols <- get.interval.cols()
deprecated <- c("sparse_auclast", "sparse_auc_se", "sparse_auc_df", "sparse_aumclast",
                "sparse_aumc_se", "sparse_aumc_df", "cl.sparse.last", "mrt.sparse.last",
                "kel.sparse.last", "vss.sparse.last", "vz.sparse.last")
has_sparse_fun <- vapply(cols, function(x) !is.na(x$FUN_sparse), logical(1))
d_sparse_estimators <- data.frame(
  parameter = names(cols)[has_sparse_fun],
  FUN_sparse = vapply(cols[has_sparse_fun], `[[`, character(1), "FUN_sparse"),
  description = vapply(cols[has_sparse_fun], `[[`, character(1), "desc")
)
d_sparse_estimators |>
  filter(!parameter %in% deprecated) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)

# Sparse-only parameters: the _se and _df companions
d_param <- pknca_parameter_table()
setdiff(d_param$parameter[d_param$sparse], deprecated)
```

Every other parameter is calculated from the arithmetic-mean profile.

---

## Deprecated parameter names

Sparse calculations used to be requested through a parallel set of names. All eleven still calculate and give the values they always gave, but each warns (once per session) and **will be an error in the next minor release of PKNCA** (≥ 0.13.0). Only the first three were in a release (0.12.1 and earlier).

| Deprecated | Use instead |
|---|---|
| `sparse_auclast` | `auclast` |
| `sparse_auc_se` | `auclast_se` |
| `sparse_auc_df` | `auclast_df` |
| `sparse_aumclast` | `aumclast` |
| `sparse_aumc_se` | `aumclast_se` |
| `sparse_aumc_df` | `aumclast_df` |
| `cl.sparse.last` | `cl.last` |
| `mrt.sparse.last` | `mrt.last` |
| `kel.sparse.last` | `kel.last` |
| `vss.sparse.last` | `vss.last` |
| `vz.sparse.last` | `vz.last` |

Every replacement except the last gives the same number as the name it replaces. `vz.sparse.last` divided the clearance by `1/MRT`, which made it numerically identical to Vss; `vz.last` divides by the λz of the mean profile, so re-run any comparison that used `vz.sparse.last`.

The functions behind the sparse estimators (`pk.calc.sparse_auc()`, `pk.calc.sparse_auclast()`, `pk.calc.sparse_aumc()`, `pk.calc.sparse_aumclast()`, `as_sparse_pk()`, `sparse_mean()`, `var_sparse_auc()`, `var_sparse_aumc()`, and `cov_holder()`) are not deprecated and remain available for calculations outside `pk.nca()`.

---

## Key differences from dense NCA

| Aspect | Dense PK | Sparse PK |
|---|---|---|
| `PKNCAconc()` flag | `sparse = FALSE` (default) | `sparse = TRUE` |
| Samples per subject | Full individual profile | One or a few |
| Results | One row per subject per parameter | One row per group per parameter |
| AUC and AUMC (`auclast`, `aucinf.obs`, ...) | Trapezoidal rule per subject, `auc.method` | Sparse estimator, linear trapezoidal only |
| Standard error and df | Not available | `_se` and `_df` companions |
| Other parameters (Cmax, half-life, ...) | Per subject | From the arithmetic-mean profile |
| Concentration at time 0 | Measured or any imputation | Measured, or a zero (`start_conc0`); C0 back-extrapolated for IV parameters |
| Uncertainty of derived parameters | Between-subject summary statistics | `sparse_bootstrap()` |

Bailer AJ. Testing for the equality of area under the curves when using destructive measurement techniques. *J Pharmacokinet Biopharm*. 1988;16(3):303-309.

Holder DJ, Hsuan F, Dixit R, Soper K. A method for estimating and testing area under the curve in serial sacrifice, batch, and complete data designs. *J Biopharm Stat*. 1999;9(3):451-464.

Holder DJ. Comments on Nedelman and Jia's extension of Satterthwaite's approximation applied to pharmacokinetics. *J Biopharm Stat*. 2001;11(1-2):75-79.

Nedelman JR, Gibiansky E, Lau DTW. Applying Bailer's method for AUC confidence intervals to sparse sampling. *Pharm Res*. 1995;12(1):124-128.

Nedelman JR, Jia X. An extension of Satterthwaite's approximation applied to pharmacokinetics. *J Biopharm Stat*. 1998;8(2):317-328.

Shen M, Machado SG. Bioequivalence evaluation of sparse sampling pharmacokinetics data using bootstrap resampling method. *J Biopharm Stat*. 2017;27(2):257-264.

Takemoto S, Yamaoka K, Nishikawa M, Takakura Y. Histogram analysis of pharmacokinetic parameters by bootstrap resampling from one-point sampling data in animal experiments. *Drug Metab Pharmacokinet*. 2006;21(6):458-464.
